newsitem.title: USA: Gillette buying Duracell for $7 billion.
newsitem.headline: Gillette buying Duracell for $7 billion.

text.p: Gillette Co., the shaving products powerhouse, made a big leap into the wider consumer products market Thursday, saying it will acquire battery maker Duracell International Inc. for about $7 billion in stock.

The merger, expected to quickly add to Boston-based Gillette's earnings, brings together two household names whose products are frequently seen side by side on store shelves and in checkout counters across the United States.

Gillette Chairman Alfred Zeien said the acquisition was expected to yield between $80 million and $120 million in savings in two years. He added that the deal will add to Gillette's earnings "from day one," although he did not offer a specific figure.

"Duracell is already the world leader in the highly profitable and fast-growing alkaline battery market, and has the potential to grow that share in association with the Gillette worldwide marketing and distribution organisation," Zeien said in a statement.
Wall Street analysts and investors welcomed the deal.
Duracell's stock gained $9 to $58.125 while Gillette added $1 to $66, both on the New York Stock Exchange.
"It's a good deal for both companies. It gives Gillette a sixth core business ... (and) the merchandizing possibilities are tremendous," said Edward D. Jones analyst Tony Vento.
Founded in 1901, Gillette is the world leader in male grooming products, a category that includes razors and blades, shaving preparations and electric shavers.
It is also the world's top seller of toothbrushes and oral care appliances with its Oral-B line. It also makes Parker pens and Braun shavers and other appliances.
Duracell International is the world's leading manufacturer of alkaline batteries. It also markets rechargeable battery packs, primary lithium batteries and zinc air batteries.

While Gillette's razors and other products, such as toothbrushes and pens, are often found right next to Duracell batteries in U.S. stores, Gillette has a far better distribution network overseas, analysts said.
"Duracell sales will accelerate because of this," said Vento. Gillette is particularly strong in Latin America and other developing markets, where Bethel, Conn.-based Duracell is not as well known.

Bear Stearns & Co. analyst Constance Maneaty, who follows both companies, noted Duracell that "is the worldwide leader in alkaline battery sales. And once Duracell is fully intergrated with Gillette, they will get into more locations than they've been."
Moody's Investor Services analyst Joseph Chakra said the deal would also give Gillette entry into new U.S. outlets.
"Right now, Duracell is sold in toy stores. Maybe this will provide an entree for one of Gillette's products, like pens," he said. Gillette owns both Parker and Paper-Mate pens.
Chakra noted that prior to Gillette's acquisition of Oral-B tooth brushes, "they weren't in pharmacies."
The transaction, which is intended to be a tax-free exchange of shares, still needs the approval of stockholders of both companies, which is expected.

Buyout specialists Kohlberg Kravis & Roberts Co., L.P., which owns about 34 percent of Duracell's outstanding shares, agreed to vote in favour of the merger. That is not surprising. KKR has turned an initial $350 million investment in Duracell into more than $3 billion, a spokeswoman said.
Gillette said it will issue about 108 million shares in the stock transaction, in which Duracell stockholders will received 0.904 share of Gillette for each Duracell share they own.
